Google Health OAuth

On this page
  • Decision
  • Supported authorization flow
  • Reauthorization contract
  • Reliability invariants

Decision

MTL Explorer supports a user-owned Google Cloud project in Testing status. The user adds the Google account that holds the health data as a test user and creates a Desktop app OAuth client.

Testing-mode refresh tokens expire after seven days. MTL Explorer must treat regular reauthorization as part of the normal product flow, not as an unusual error. Testing is the permanent setup, not a temporary step: users do not publish the app, move it to In production, or have it verified by Google.

Supported authorization flow

  • Request offline access with PKCE S256, a random single-use state, and prompt=consent.
  • Redirect to the dead loopback address http://127.0.0.1:1/mtl-explorer-oauth.
  • Tell the user that the browser error is expected.
  • Accept the complete address copied from the browser. Validate its host, port, authorization result, and state before exchanging the code.
  • Use the same redirect URI for authorization and token exchange.
  • Read refresh_token_expires_in from the authorization-code token response when Google supplies it. Store the calculated expiry with the connection and return it in connection status.
  • Encrypt the refresh token at rest and keep access tokens in memory.

The complete URL is required. Unlike a bare authorization code, it lets MTL Explorer validate the OAuth state.

Why loopback and manual return

Google Desktop clients allow HTTP loopback callbacks, not arbitrary LAN or remote server URLs. localhost / 127.0.0.1 refers to the browser's device, which may differ from the MTL Explorer host. Detecting the GUI's browser URL cannot bypass this restriction. The unused loopback address and manual paste let NAS and remote installations connect without a local helper or HTTPS setup.

Automatic return to a remote server requires a Web application client with an exactly registered HTTPS callback; non-loopback IP addresses are rejected. See Google's Desktop redirect rules and Web redirect rules.

Token storage and recovery

The refresh-token encryption key is derived from the configured OAuth client secret, which stays outside the database. This protects a database-only copy; it does not protect against access to both the database and server secrets. Changing the client secret makes existing ciphertext unreadable. Reauthorize after changing it; mirrored records are retained. The access-token refresh handler logs decryption failures and marks the connection for reconnection. An unreadable token can also indicate corruption, so the UI must not claim a client-secret change as the only cause.

Advanced proxy callback

The optional Web-client callback accepts an unauthenticated GET because the return from Google cannot carry the browser's MTL Explorer authorization header. An authenticated request must first create the random state and server-held PKCE verifier. The callback consumes that state once, within ten minutes, before exchanging a code. Missing, expired, or replayed state cannot change the connection. The manual completion endpoint remains authenticated.

Reauthorization contract

The initial setup must explain that the user will normally reconnect every seven days. MTL Explorer must then:

  1. If Google reports a refresh-token expiry, show it as soon as setup finishes and use it to schedule an Admin action before authorization is lost. Do not invent an expiry when Google omits the field.
  2. Detect an expired or revoked refresh token and set RECONNECT_REQUIRED. The timer may provide an earlier reminder, but an OAuth failure remains authoritative.
  3. Classify an invalid_grant close to the recorded expiry as a likely Testing-mode expiration. Other causes, including revocation, remain possible and must not be hidden.
  4. Show an action-needed notification using the existing Admin overview and Import & sync status patterns.
  5. Provide a direct Reauthorize action and prepare a new Google consent link. Do not send the user through the complete setup assistant again.
  6. Reuse the configured client ID and client secret. The user only completes Google consent and pastes the returned loopback URL.
  7. Require a new refresh token when recovering from RECONNECT_REQUIRED; never fall back to the token known to be invalid.
  8. Replace the stored token, clear any cached access token, clear the error, keep the local mirror and track associations, and start synchronization.

An expiry warning can say:

This Google authorization expires on September 8 because the OAuth project appears to be in Testing. Reauthorize Google to keep syncing.

The supported action is Reauthorize. Moving the project to In production is not supported.

Reauthorization must not delete or duplicate the connection, mirrored health records, imported routes, or user-owned track data.

Reliability invariants

  • Resolve users/me/identity after authorization and persist its stable healthUserId. Refuse a different account when the mirror contains records, source metadata, synchronization audits/work, or retained route ownership.
  • Use one time domain for both a Google window and its authoritative deletion. Exercise uses civil start time; physical records use instants; daily rollups use dates. Offset and daylight-saving changes must not move records outside the replacement window.
  • Persist a rotated refresh token returned during access-token refresh while holding the same refresh lock.
  • On 401, or Google's structured MISSING_OAUTH_SCOPE response, invalidate the cached access token and retry once. Do not treat every 403 as stale authorization; distinguish missing scope, project policy, and disabled API.
  • Persist pagination progress. Stop an incomplete window when a page token repeats or the configured page limit is reached. Never run authoritative deletion for an incomplete window.
  • Only structured INVALID_PAGE_TOKEN responses restart a historical token traversal with smaller bounds. Other 400s remain request failures. Work retries are durable; exhausted ranges park without authorizing deletion or final marks.
  • Validate every successful page before persistence: the root must be an object, collections must be arrays of objects, page tokens must be bounded strings, and a page must not exceed the requested result limit. A missing collection remains valid because ProtoJSON normally omits empty repeated fields; {} can therefore be a legitimate empty Google response and cannot be rejected as malformed.
  • Honor both delta-seconds and HTTP-date forms of Retry-After, with bounded retry delays.
  • Log job and phase lifecycle, bounded progress milestones, final counts, and durations at INFO. Keep page-level detail and repeated recoverable stack traces at DEBUG. Log recoverable exceptions once with safe context and log terminal failures at ERROR with the throwable.
  • Report current-pass progress separately from the local mirror summary. The server calculates the exact unique row count and earliest/latest record time across both mirror tables. The database projection remains in the persistence package and is mapped to a separate web response DTO. Mirror-wide aggregate queries for status, per-type summaries, and sources are cached for five minutes while work is active, refreshed as soon as a new job completes, and invalidated when the mirror is deleted.

See synchronization for work policies and checkpoints.
